new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Awjila has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so nothing to agree or disagree with. Relative to the grammar (work 1) this footnote adds a caveat: the final-syllable accent on closed heavy syllables in Paradisi's data may be a transcription artefact rather than a genuine accent shift; the article makes no positive statement of placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The article states no accent rule of its own. It notes that in Paradisi's (1960) material every word-final closed syllable with a long vowel is transcribed as accented (i.e. the final-heavy-syllable accent of the grammar's default rule), and that the Facebook writers' failure to write those long vowels might reflect an accent shift or, more likely, Paradisi's mishearing of final CVC syllables as accented. Para 11 also mentions vowels being omitted 'especially in unstressed closed syllables', which presupposes a stressed/unstressed distinction but says nothing about placement.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the footnote is a reliability caveat on the final-heavy-syllable accent of Paradisi's transcriptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Berber of the Awjila oasis (Cyrenaica, eastern Libya), i.e. awji1241 itself, based on Umberto Paradisi's 1960 texts and word list (plus Beguinot's 1920s notes, and 2013-15 Facebook posts by Awjila residents for work 0). new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Awjila with an empty rule and no existing statements; this grammar supplies the rule (final if final syllable heavy, else penultimate; domain = accent unit including clitics; small lexical-accent class; perfective marked by final accent). Nothing in the catalog to contradict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level (accent-unit-level) accent, phonemic. Default rule: accent on the final syllable if the accent unit ends in a heavy syllable (-VC, -VCC, or -əCC); otherwise on the penultimate syllable. Because clitics (possessives, demonstratives, object markers, future a= and resultative =a, negative ur=) belong to the accent unit, adding a suffix or clitic moves the accent (təɣarìt, pl. təɣari-wìn, təɣari-win=ìyək). A small set of lexical items carry 'phonological' (lexical) accent on the other of the last two syllables; that lexical accent is lost in favour of the default when a plural suffix, clitic or PNG marking is added. In verbs, final phonological accent marks the perfective as against the sequential perfective (yufá 'he found' vs tùfa 'and she found').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; only one accent per accent unit is described.
new_statements.exceptions: Nominal lexical accent on the final syllable: verbal nouns of the c*, vc*, c̄* types (agú 'doing', əččú 'food', əssú, əggú, əžžú, ufú 'finding', uɣú 'taking', ušú 'coming', explained by a lost Proto-Berber *ʔ), plus təžə́r 'moon', təvə́l 'sheep', avú 'smoke', atəlá 'linseed', izí n agmàr 'horse fly'; lexical accent on the penultimate in only two words, tfíɣit 'animal excrement' and tqə́rṭay 'paper' (p. 45). Some words appear with default accent in Paradisi's texts but lexical accent in his word list (tĕkábęrt ~ tĕkabę́rt 'shirt', arennú ~ arénnu). Reliability caveat p. 50: Paradisi mis-transcribed Zuara Berber by placing accent on word-final CVC syllables (10 of 25 discrepancies), so "This rule must therefore be treated with some care"; but p. 51 finds his Awjila accents consistent with Beguinot's (35 of 49 shared items identical, 3 differ).
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Berber of the Awjila oasis (Cyrenaica, eastern Libya), i.e. awji1241 itself, based on Umberto Paradisi's 1960 texts and word list (plus Beguinot's 1920s notes, and 2013-15 Facebook posts by Awjila residents for work 0). The archive.org copy of work 1 is the 2013 Leiden dissertation version of the 2014 Koeppe book (same title and author, 361 pp., handle 1887/21848); the accent section is 2.5 and its page numbers match the citation 'Van Putten 2014: 50' given in work 0, so the text appears to be essentially identical to the print edition. Section 2.5.3.1 discusses Zuara Berber (zuar1237-type, NW Libya) only as a check on Paradisi's transcription reliability, not as a description of Awjila.

readall_conflicts: No direct conflict between the two works, but a reliability caveat: van Putten 2014 (pp. 46-51) itself shows that Paradisi, the sole substantial source, tended to hear accent on word-final CVC syllables in Zuara Berber where it does not belong, so the final-heavy-syllable half of the default rule 'must be treated with some care', while his Awjila accents agree well with Beguinot's independent notations. Van Putten & Souag 2015 (fn. 7) lean the same way: the Facebook writers' omission of long vowels in final closed syllables 'might suggest Awjila has undergone an accent shift, or, more likely, that Paradisi misheard vowels as accented in this context'. So the final-syllable branch of the weight rule rests on Paradisi's ear; the penultimate default and the lexical-accent class are better supported.

tone.quote: Berber languages of Morocco and Algeria (except Tuareg) do not seem to have a system of word accent. Instead, accentual features are governed by higher level prosodic organization, which one could call intonation. The situation is different in the Berber languages of Libya and Egypt, and in Tuareg. ... Van Putten (2014a) provides us with a well-argued overview of the system in Awjila based on older literature, while Mitchell (2009) gives due attention to accentual factors in Zwara. ... As shown by Brugnatelli (1986), a number of Libyan varieties have stem-initial accent in the Aorist of disyllabic verbs, while the accent is on the second syllable of such verbs in the Perfective.
